title: How to Choose a Digital Marketing Agency in Dubai: 10 Questions to Ask
metaTitle: How to Choose a Digital Marketing Agency in Dubai
metaDescription: Ten questions that separate a dependable Dubai marketing agency from a risky one: proof, reporting, account ownership, Arabic capability and contracts.
excerpt: Dubai has no shortage of marketing agencies, and most proposals look alike. These ten questions cut through the pitch: who does the work, what proof they can show, who owns your accounts, and how you will know it is working.

faqs.q: What should I look for in a digital marketing agency in Dubai?
faqs.a: Look for documented results in a business like yours, clarity about who does the work, reporting you can verify in your own accounts, ownership of your ad accounts and data, real Arabic capability if you sell to Arabic speakers, and a contract with a clear scope and a reasonable exit. An agency that is strong on these is usually strong on the rest.

faqs.q: How long should I commit to a marketing agency?
faqs.a: Paid advertising can be judged within a few months, while SEO usually needs three to six months before results are clear. A sensible first contract runs three to six months with a clear notice period afterwards. Be cautious about twelve-month lock-ins with no exit clause before the agency has proven anything.

faqs.q: Should I choose a specialist agency or a full-service agency?
faqs.a: A specialist suits a business with one clear need and an in-house team to cover the rest. A full-service agency suits a business that needs several channels to work together, for example ads, SEO, creative and the website, because one team can fix a problem wherever it sits. Ask a full-service agency to show proof in each service you plan to buy.

faqs.q: Who should own the ad accounts and analytics?
faqs.a: You should. Ad accounts, analytics, Search Console and the website should be registered to your business, with the agency given access. That way your data, history and audiences stay with you if you change agency. Agencies that insist on running your campaigns from their own accounts make leaving expensive.

body:
Dubai is one of the most competitive marketing markets in the world, and choosing an agency here is hard for a simple reason: every proposal promises growth, and most look the same. The differences only show up months later, in the results and in how the relationship works.

These ten questions bring those differences forward. Ask them before you sign.

## 1. What results can you show for a business like mine?

Ask for case studies in your industry or one close to it, with numbers: where the client started, what was done, and where they ended up, over what period. Vague claims such as "we increased engagement" tell you nothing.

Good proof is specific. For example, a case study that says organic traffic grew from 22,000 to 350,000 monthly sessions over twelve months, and explains how, can be questioned and checked. Look through an agency's [case studies](/case-studies/) before the first call, and ask about the ones closest to your situation.

## 2. Who will actually do the work?

Many agencies sell with senior people and deliver with juniors or subcontractors. Neither is wrong in itself, but you should know.

Ask who will manage your account, who writes the content, who builds the campaigns and who designs the creative. Ask whether they are employees or freelancers, and whether you can speak to them. An in-house team that sits together fixes problems faster, because the person running your ads can walk over to the person who builds your landing pages.

## 3. How will you report, and can I verify it?

A report should show what was done, what it cost and what it produced, in numbers you can check yourself in Google Analytics, Search Console and your ad accounts.

Ask to see a sample report. Be wary of reports built on metrics that sound good but do not connect to revenue, such as impressions or follower counts on their own.

## 4. Who owns the accounts and the data?

Your ad accounts, analytics, Search Console property and website should belong to your business, with the agency given access. This matters most on the day you leave. If the agency owns the ad account, you lose the campaign history, audiences and tracking, and start again from nothing.

## 5. What is included, and what costs extra?

Get the scope in writing: how many campaigns, how much content, how many creative assets, how many hours. Ask what is not included. Common surprises are ad creative, landing pages, video production and tracking setup.

Ad spend is separate from the agency fee. Make sure the proposal shows both, and how the fee is calculated.

## 6. Can you work in Arabic, natively?

A large share of UAE and Gulf buyers search, read and buy in Arabic. Translating English campaigns word for word does not work: the keywords differ, the tone differs, and right-to-left layout needs care.

If Arabic speakers are part of your market, ask who writes the Arabic content and whether they are native speakers. Ask for examples of Arabic campaigns or pages they have ranked. Our [Arabic SEO guide](/blog/arabic-seo-guide/) explains why this is one of the largest untapped opportunities in the region.

## 7. How do you decide what to do first?

A good agency starts with an audit of where you are: your website, your tracking, your current campaigns and your competitors. Then it prioritises. If a proposal offers the same package it offers everyone, without questions about your margins, your customers or your goals, the work will be generic too.

Ask what they would do in the first thirty days and why.

## 8. What happens if results do not come?

Honest agencies do not guarantee rankings or a fixed return, because nobody controls Google or the ad auctions. What they can commit to is the work, the reporting and a process for changing course.

Ask how they have handled an account that underperformed. The answer tells you more than any success story.

## 9. What are the contract terms?

Check the minimum term, the notice period, and what happens to your accounts and assets at the end. A three- to six-month initial term is reasonable for most services, because [SEO](/marketing/seo/) in particular needs time to show results. A twelve-month lock-in with no exit, signed before any work is proven, mostly benefits the agency.

## 10. Do your services work together?

Marketing channels depend on each other. Ads send traffic to a website, the website has to convert it, SEO needs developers to implement fixes, and all of it needs creative. When these sit in separate companies, problems fall between them.

Ask how the agency handles the handovers. If it offers [performance marketing](/marketing/performance-marketing/), SEO, creative and development under one roof, ask how those teams actually work together day to day.

## Warning signs

- Guaranteed number-one rankings or guaranteed returns.
- No access to your own ad accounts or analytics.
- Reports that never mention revenue or leads.
- Pressure to sign a long contract quickly.
- Case studies with no numbers and no detail.
- Reluctance to let you speak to the people doing the work.

## How to compare proposals

Put the proposals side by side and compare the same things: scope, people, reporting, ownership, contract terms and proof. The cheapest proposal is often the one with the least work in it, and the most expensive is not automatically the best.

Then have a real conversation with the shortlist. How an agency answers these ten questions matters as much as what it answers. Straight, specific answers are a good sign. Deflection is not.
